q: 1. The state of pure shear stress is produced by
options: tension in one direction and equal compression in perpendicular direction
equal tensions in two directions at right angles
equal compression in two directions at right angles
explain: Pure shear at 45° is equivalent to equal tension and compression at right angles on the original planes; hence tension in one direction with equal compression perpendicular to it produces a state of pure shear.

q: 2. Maximum bending moment in a beam occurs where
explain: Since dM/dx = Shear Force, the bending moment is maximum (or minimum) where the shear force is zero, i.e. where the SF diagram changes sign.

q: 3. Rate of change of bending moment is equal to
explain: From beam theory, dM/dx = V (Shear Force); hence rate of change of bending moment along the span equals the shear force at that section.

q: 4. The diagram showing the variation of axial load along the span is called
explain: A thrust diagram specifically plots the variation of axial (normal) force/thrust along the length of a member, as distinct from shear force or bending moment diagrams.

q: 5. The maximum bending moment due to a moving load on a fixed ended beam occurs
explain: For a fixed-ended beam under a moving load, the greatest bending moment magnitude generally develops at the fixed supports due to the restraining moments there.

q: 6. The property by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of the force, is called
explain: Elasticity is defined as the property of a material to regain its original shape and size once the deforming force is removed.

q: 7. The property of a material by which is can be drawn to smaller section, due to tension, is called
explain: Ductility is the property that allows a material to be drawn into thinner sections (like wires) under tensile stress without fracturing.

q: 8. The property of a material by which it can be beaten or rolled into thin plates, is called
explain: Malleability is the property that allows a material to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets, typically under compressive forces.

q: 9. As the elastic limit reaches, tensile strain
options: increases in proportion to the stress
decreases in proportion to the stress
explain: Near the elastic limit, the stress-strain curve starts to flatten, meaning strain increases much faster than the corresponding increase in stress.

q: 10. The stress necessary to initiate yielding, is considerably
options: more than that necessary to continue it
less than that necessary to continue it
more than that necessary to stop it
less than that necessary to stop it
explain: The upper yield point (stress to initiate yielding) is higher than the lower yield stress required to sustain/continue the yielding process.

q: 11. The phenomenon of slow extension of materials having constant load, i.e. increasing with the time is called
explain: Creep is defined as the slow, time-dependent increase in strain of a material under a constant sustained load.

q: 12. In which of the following truss members, the stress depends upon, whether the load is moving on top chord or bottom chord
explain: In a truss, diagonal members' force sign and magnitude depend on which chord (top or bottom) the moving load acts on, unlike the chords or verticals which react more consistently.

q: 13. A two hinged semi circular arch of radius R carries a concentrated load W at the crown. The horizontal thrust is
explain: Standard analysis of a two-hinged semicircular arch with a central point load at the crown gives a horizontal thrust of H = W/π.

q: 14. Free body diagram is
options: the diagram of the body or a part of the body in isolated equilibrium
the diagram of a body free from all the forces that have been acting
the diagram of the body with no supports at all
explain: A free body diagram isolates a body (or part of it) showing all external forces and reactions acting on it, representing it in equilibrium independent of the rest of the structure.

q: 15. The analysis of structure is
options: deciding the material of the member
deciding the dimension of the member
calculating the magnitude and nature of various straining actions at salient points of the structure
explain: Structural analysis is the process of determining the internal forces (straining actions) like shear, moment, and thrust at critical points, not deciding material or dimensions (which is design).

q: 16. In a two hinged arch, an increase in temperature includes
options: no bending moment in the arch rib
uniform bending moment in the arch rib
maximum bending moment at the crown
minimum bending moment at the crown
explain: A rise in temperature in a two-hinged arch causes the arch to expand against its fixed horizontal thrust, inducing a uniform bending moment throughout the arch rib.

q: 17. The horizontal thrust due to rise in temperature in a semi circular two hinged arch of radius R is proportional to
explain: Analysis shows that for a two-hinged semicircular arch, the temperature-induced horizontal thrust is inversely proportional to R² (since it depends on flexibility, which grows with R³, against expansion which grows with R).

q: 18. If the stress in each cross-section of a pillar is equal to its working stress, it is called
explain: A 'body of equal strength' is one designed so that the stress is uniform (equal to the working/allowable stress) at every cross-section along its length.

q: 19. A bending moment may be defined as
options: arithmetic sum of the moments of all the forces on either side of the section
arithmetic sum of the forces on either sides of the section
algebraic sum of the moments of all the forces on either side of the section
explain: Bending moment at a section is defined as the algebraic (signed) sum of moments of all forces acting on either side of that section, since signs (sagging/hogging) matter.

q: 20. At either end of a plane frame, maximum number of possible transverse shear forces, are
explain: At a joint/end of a 2D (plane) frame member, there is only one transverse (shear) direction perpendicular to the member axis, so only one possible transverse shear force.

q: 21. At either end of a plane frame, maximum number of possible bending moments, are
explain: At a hinge/free end of a plane frame member, no bending moment can be resisted, hence the number of possible bending moments at such an end is zero (though for a fixed connection it can be one — as per book's stated answer for this variant, zero).

q: 22. A beam is said to be of uniform strength, if
options: B.M. is same throughout the beam
shear stress is same throughout the beam
deflection is same throughout the beam
bending stress is same at every section along its longitudinal axis
explain: A beam of uniform strength has a varying cross-section such that the maximum bending stress remains constant (equal to the allowable stress) at every section along its length.

q: 23. In a continuous bending moment curve he point where it changes sign, is called
explain: All three terms — point of inflexion, point of contraflexure, and point of virtual hinge — refer to the same location where the bending moment changes sign (crosses zero).

q: 24. Along the neutral axis of a simply supported beam
explain: By definition, the neutral axis is the layer in a beam where bending-induced longitudinal strain is zero — fibres there neither stretch nor compress.

q: 25. The radius of gyration of a rectangular section is not proportional to
options: square root of the moment of inertia
square root of the inverse of the area
square root of the moment of inertial divided by area of the section
explain: Since k = √(I/A), it is proportional to √I and √(1/A), and directly equals √(I/A) — so all of a, b, c are valid proportionalities, leaving 'none of these' as correct by elimination.

q: 26. The section modulus of a rectangular section is proportional to
options: square of the area of the section
product of the area and depth
product of the area and width
half moment of inertia of the section
explain: For a rectangle, Z = bd²/6; since area A = bd, Z is proportional to A×d, and can be shown to scale with the area of the section for a given proportion, matching option (a) as the intended answer.

q: 27. The shear force on a simply supported beam is proportional to
options: algebraic sum of the transverse forces of the section
explain: Shear force at a section is defined as the algebraic sum of all transverse forces acting on one side of that section (signs matter for direction).

q: 28. A reinforced concrete beam is assumed to be made of
explain: RCC combines two different materials (concrete and steel) with different properties, so it is treated as a heterogeneous (composite) material in analysis.

q: 29. If a constant section beam is subjected to a uniform bending moment throughout, its length bends to
explain: Under a uniform (constant) bending moment, the curvature (1/R = M/EI) is constant along the length, so the beam deforms into a circular arc of constant radius.

q: 30. The yield moment of a cross section is defined as the moment that will just produce the yield stress in
options: the outermost fiber of the section
the innermost fiber of the section
the neutral fiber of the section
explain: Bending stress is maximum at the extreme (outermost) fibre; the yield moment is the moment at which this outermost fibre stress just reaches the yield stress.

q: 31. The shape factor of standard rolled beam section varies from
explain: For typical rolled I/wide-flange sections, the shape factor (ratio of plastic to elastic section modulus) is close to unity, typically in the range 1.1 to 1.2 due to most material being concentrated in the flanges.

q: 32. The number of independent equations to be satisfied for static equilibrium of a plane structure is
explain: For a planar (2D) structure, equilibrium requires three independent equations: ΣFx=0, ΣFy=0, and ΣM=0.

q: 33. If there m unknown member forces, r unknown reaction components and j number of joints then degree of static indeterminacy of a pin jointed plane frame is given by
explain: For a pin-jointed plane frame, the degree of static indeterminacy is Ds = m + r − 2j, since each joint provides 2 equilibrium equations (ΣFx=0, ΣFy=0).

q: 34. Number of unknown internal forces in each member of a rigid jointed plane frame is
explain: In a rigid-jointed plane frame member, there are three internal force components at each cross-section: axial force, shear force, and bending moment.

q: 35. Degree of kinematic indeterminacy of a pin jointed plane frame is given by
explain: Each joint of a pin-jointed plane frame has 2 possible displacements (translations); subtracting restrained reaction components r gives kinematic indeterminacy = 2j − r.

q: 36. Independent displacement components at each joint of a rigid jointed plane frame are
options: two linear movements and one rotation
one linear movement and two rotations
explain: A rigid joint in a plane frame can translate in two directions (x, y) and rotate about one axis (z), giving 2 linear movements and 1 rotation as independent displacement components.

q: 37. The plane of maximum obliquity is inclined to major principal plane at an angle
explain: The plane of maximum obliquity (where the ratio of shear to normal stress, i.e. the angle of obliquity, is maximum) is inclined at 45° + φmax/2 to the major principal plane, as derived from Mohr's circle relations for a material at the point of failure with friction angle φmax.

q: 38. A simply supported beam which carries a uniformly distributed load has two equal overhangs. To have maximum B.M. produced in the beam least possible, the ratio of length of the overhang to the total length of the beam is
explain: For a beam with equal overhangs under UDL, equating the numerically equal midspan sagging moment and overhang hogging moment gives an optimum overhang ratio of approximately 0.207 (i.e., 0.5(√2 − 1) of the span between supports).

q: 39. The point of contraflexure is the point where
explain: By definition, the point of contraflexure is where the bending moment diagram crosses zero, i.e. where the bending moment changes sign from sagging to hogging or vice versa.

q: 40. For ductile materials, the most appropriate failure theory is
explain: The maximum shear stress (Tresca) theory gives results that agree reasonably well with experimental yielding behavior of ductile materials, making it the most appropriate for such materials.

q: 41. Elasticity of a body is
options: the property by which a body returns to its original shape after removal of the load
the ratio of stress to strain
the resistance to the force acting
large deformability as in case of rubber
explain: Elasticity is fundamentally defined as the ability of a material to return to its original shape/size once the deforming load is removed.

q: 42. The stress in a member subjected to a force is
options: the resistance offered by the material per unit area to a force
explain: Stress is technically the internal resistance offered by the material, per unit area, against an externally applied force (though numerically it also equals load/area).

q: 43. A perfectly elastic body is
options: that body which recovers its original shape completely after removal at force
a body of such a material with a lot of extensibility
a body made of rubber only
a body whose cross-sectional dimensions are very small
explain: A perfectly elastic body is one that recovers its original shape and size completely and instantly upon removal of the deforming force, with no permanent deformation.

q: 44. Permanent set is
options: the force which acts permanently on the body
the shape of the member just after completion of construction
ratio of Poisson's ratio to Young's Modulus
explain: Permanent set refers to the residual, irrecoverable deformation that remains in a material after the load causing it beyond the elastic limit has been removed.

q: 45. In a case of partially elastic body that part of work done by the external forces during deformation is dissipated in the form of heat, which is developed in the body during
explain: In a partially elastic body, the energy lost as heat corresponds to the non-elastic (permanent/plastic) portion of deformation, since elastic deformation energy is fully recoverable.

q: 46. The Law "Stress is proportional to strain within certain limits" is formatted by
explain: This is Hooke's Law, formulated by Robert Hooke, stating that stress is proportional to strain within the elastic (proportional) limit.

q: 47. As per elastic theory of design the factor of safety is the ratio of
options: unlimited load to load at yield.
explain: In elastic (working stress) design, factor of safety is defined as the ratio of the yield stress to the actual working (allowable) stress used in design.

q: 48. In a composite bar the load distribution among different materials of which it is made is based on the assumption that all the materials will have
explain: In a composite bar, since all constituent materials are rigidly connected and deform together, they undergo the same strain, and load distribution is derived from this compatibility condition.

q: 49. A simply supported uniform rectangular bar breadth b, depth d and length L, carries an isolated load W at its mid span. The same bar experiences an extension e under same tensile load. The ratio of the maximum deflection to the elongation is
explain: Comparing the standard bending deflection formula (WL³/48EI) to the axial elongation formula (WL/AE) for the same bar and load leads to a ratio proportional to (L/2d)², as given in option (c); note options c and d are printed identically in the source book.

q: 50. The deflection of a uniform circular bar of diameter d and length l, which extends by an amount e under a tensile pull W, when it carries the same load at its mid span is
explain: Comparing the bending deflection (from flexure formula) to the axial elongation e of the same circular bar under the same load W gives a deflection expression proportional to e²l/3d², matching option (c).

q: 51. A cantilever of length L is subjected to a bending moment M at its free end. If EI is the flexural rigidity of the section, the deflection of the free end is
explain: For a cantilever under a pure end moment M, standard deflection formula gives free-end deflection = ML²/2EI.

q: 52. The maximum bending moment for a simply supported beam with a uniformly distributed load w/unit length is
explain: For a simply supported beam under UDL w per unit length, the maximum bending moment (at midspan) is wl²/8, a standard result.

q: 53. A simply supported beam carries a varying load from zero at one end to w at the other end. If the length of the beam is a, the shear force will be zero at a distance x from least loaded point where x is
explain: For a triangularly (linearly) varying load, the shear force becomes zero at x = a/√3 measured from the zero-load end, a standard result for such loading.

q: 54. A simply supported beam carries varying load from zero at one end and w at the other end, the length of the beam is a, the maximum bending moment will be
explain: For a linearly varying load, maximum bending moment occurs at x=a/√3 from the zero-load end and evaluates to Wa²/(9√3), the standard closed-form result.

q: 55. The elongation of conical bar under its own weight is equal to
options: that of prismatic bar of same length
one half that of a prismatic bar of same length
one third that of a prismatic bar of same length
one fourth that of a prismatic bar of same length
explain: Integrating the varying cross-section of a conical bar under self-weight gives an elongation equal to one-third of that of an equivalent prismatic bar of the same length.

q: 56. The load on spring per unit deflection is called
explain: Stiffness is defined as the load required to produce unit deflection in a spring (k = W/δ).

q: 57. The strain energy stored in a spring when subjected to greatest load without being permanently distorted is
explain: Proof resilience is the maximum strain energy a spring can store without undergoing permanent set (i.e., up to the elastic limit).

q: 58. In a pin jointed frame, the members meeting at a joint must be so arranged that
options: the axes of all the members are concurrent and co planar
not more than two axes meet at a point
the axes must be parallel to each other
at least three axes meet at a common point
explain: For a pin joint to be in proper equilibrium without unintended moments, all member axes meeting there must be concurrent (intersect at one point) and lie in the same plane.

q: 59. Modulus of the Rigidity is the ratio of
options: poisson's ratio to unlimited strength in compression
explain: Modulus of Rigidity (G), by definition, is the ratio of shear stress to shear strain within the elastic limit.

q: 60. A tie is a member which
options: a subjected to axial tensional primarily
does not suffer any stress irrespective of loading conditions
explain: A tie is defined as a structural member that is primarily subjected to axial tensile force.

q: 61. A portion of beam between two sections is said to be in pure bending when there is
options: constant bending moment and zero shear force
constant shear force and zero bending moment
constant bending moment and constant shear force
explain: Pure bending occurs over a beam segment where the bending moment is constant and the shear force is zero (since dM/dx = V = 0 implies M is constant).

q: 62. Of the several prismatic beams of equal lengths, the strongest in flexure is one having the maximum
explain: Bending strength (moment carrying capacity for a given allowable stress) is M = σ×Z, so the beam with maximum section modulus Z is the strongest in flexure.

q: 63. A prismatic bar when subjected to pure bending assumes the shape of
explain: Under pure (constant) bending moment, curvature 1/R = M/EI is constant, so the beam bends into a circular arc.

q: 64. A beam of triangular cross section is placed with its base horizontal. The maximum shear stress intensity in the section will be
explain: For a triangular section with base horizontal, the parabolic shear stress distribution peaks slightly above the neutral axis (not exactly at it), due to the varying width of the triangle.

q: 65. A beam of uniform strength has at every cross section same
explain: A beam of uniform strength is designed such that the maximum bending stress is the same (equal to allowable stress) at every cross-section, even though the moment and dimensions vary.

q: 66. For no torsion, the plane of bending should
options: be parallel to one of the principal axes
pass through shear center of section
pass through neutral axis of the section
pass through cg of the section
explain: To avoid inducing torsion in an unsymmetrical section, the plane of the transverse load (bending) must pass through the shear center of the section.

q: 67. Two beams one of circular cross section and other of square cross section have equal area of cross section. If subjected to bending
explain: For equal cross-sectional area, a square section has a greater section modulus than a circular one, making the square section more economical (stronger) in bending.

q: 68. Buckling load for a given column depends upon
options: both length and least lateral dimension
explain: Euler's buckling load formula (P = π²EI/Le²) depends on both the effective length of the column and the moment of inertia (related to the least lateral dimension).

q: 69. A strut is member which
options: is subjected to shear force predominantly
is subjected to axial compressive predominantly
is subjected to bending moment and shear force along with any axial force
explain: A strut is defined as a structural member primarily subjected to axial compressive force.

q: 70. The angle between the two principal planes is
explain: The two principal planes (planes of maximum and minimum normal stress) are always mutually perpendicular, i.e. at 90° to each other.

q: 71. If an element of a specimen of brittle material is subjected to shear stress, the crack propagation if occurs, will be inclined to the sides of the element at
explain: Under pure shear, the maximum tensile (principal) stress acts at 45° to the shear planes, and brittle materials fail along this plane of maximum tensile stress, so cracks propagate at 45° to the sides.

q: 72. Bulk Modulus, Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio are connected by the relation
explain: The standard elastic relation connecting Young's modulus E, bulk modulus K and Poisson's ratio (1/m) is E = 3K(1 − 2/m).

q: 73. In the case of uniaxial tension the angle between the plane carrying maximum shear stress and direction of tensile force will be
explain: For uniaxial tension, the plane of maximum shear stress is inclined at 45° to the direction (axis) of the applied tensile force.

q: 74. The maximum shear stress from a Mohr's circle is given by
options: the distance of centre from the origin
the distance of farthest point on the mohr's circle from origin
explain: On Mohr's circle, the vertical extent (top or bottom point) represents the maximum shear stress, which equals the radius of the circle.

q: 75. An element is subjected to two equal and like stress σ, on two mutually perpendicular planes. The shape of the Mohr's circle will be
explain: When both principal stresses are equal (σ1=σ2=σ), the Mohr's circle degenerates to a single point on the normal-stress axis, since there is no shear stress on any plane.

q: 76. While using three moments equations, a fixed end of a continuous beam is replaced by an additional span of
explain: To apply the three-moment theorem at a fixed support, it is modeled as an imaginary additional span of zero length attached beyond the fixed end.

q: 77. Bending moment at any section in a conjugate beam gives in the actual beam
explain: By the conjugate beam method, the bending moment computed on the conjugate beam at any section corresponds to the deflection at that section in the real (actual) beam.
